topicName: Window Functions, CTEs, and Recursive Queries
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced T-SQL: Window Functions, CTEs, and Recursive Queries in Microsoft SQL Server"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Modern T-SQL development relies heavily on advanced querying constructs to solve complex analytical and hierarchical problems efficiently. In this tutorial, we will explore Common Table Expressions (CTEs), powerful Window Functions, and Recursive CTEs in Microsoft SQL Server."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Common Table Expressions (CTEs)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Common Table Expression (CTE) provides a temporary result set that you can reference within a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement. CTEs improve readability and can replace complex derived tables or views."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"WITH RegionalSales AS (
    SELECT 
        Region,
        SUM(SalesAmount) AS TotalSales
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY Region
)
SELECT 
    Region,
    TotalSales,
    CASE 
        WHEN TotalSales > 1000000 THEN 'High'
        ELSE 'Standard'
    END AS PerformanceCategory
FROM RegionalSales;
"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Window Functions"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows that are somehow related to the current row. Unlike aggregate functions, window functions do not collapse rows into a single summary row; each row retains its identity."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Ranking functions: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), and NTILE()."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Value functions: LAG(), LEAD(), FIRST_VALUE(), and LAST_VALUE()."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Aggregate window functions: SUM(), AVG(), and COUNT() used with the OVER() clause."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"SELECT 
    EmployeeID,
    Department,
    Salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Department ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS SalaryRank,
    LAG(Salary, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY Department ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS PreviousSalary
FROM Employees;
"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Recursive Queries"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"A recursive CTE is a CTE that references itself. It is extremely useful for querying hierarchical data, such as organizational charts, bill-of-materials, or folder structures. A recursive CTE consists of an anchor member, a recursive member, and a termination condition."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"WITH EmployeeHierarchy AS (
    -- Anchor Member: Top-level managers (no boss)
    SELECT 
        EmployeeID,
        ManagerID,
        EmployeeName,
        0 AS HierarchyLevel
    FROM Employees
    WHERE ManagerID IS NULL
    
    UNION ALL
    
    -- Recursive Member: Subordinates
    SELECT 
        e.EmployeeID,
        e.ManagerID,
        e.EmployeeName,
        eh.HierarchyLevel + 1
    FROM Employees e
    INNER JOIN EmployeeHierarchy eh ON e.ManagerID = eh.EmployeeID
)
SELECT 
    EmployeeID,
    ManagerID,
    EmployeeName,
    HierarchyLevel
FROM EmployeeHierarchy
ORDER BY HierarchyLevel, EmployeeName;
"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"By combining CTEs, window functions, and recursive queries, you can write highly optimized, clean, and maintainable T-SQL code to solve advanced data engineering and analytical challenges in SQL Server."}]
